content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

The outer shell 10 carries a mechanical exposure indicator 80 visible from outside the carrier 100. The core matter is well supported: shell/tray/module/lid architecture, tray feet and lower return passage, tray side walls spaced inward forming two side supply passages, rigid spacer frame with two opposed phase-change cassettes, central inlet opening, two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes, peripheral outlet openings aligned with the side supply passages, the full circulation path (rise → central inlet → divide along cassette faces → guide ducts → side supply passages → tray perforations → lower return passage), the absence of any fan, pump or powered air mover, the depending indexing rib entering the mating channel and shifting the module to the registered position, the gasket sealing after registration, the resilient feet pressed onto shell ledges, the condensate channel/wick/pull tab/duct discharge openings, and the latched, manually-reset mechanical exposure indicator that does not control airflow. findings.where: figures/FIG-6.md (cutting-plane paragraph and "View designations"); figures/FIG-7.md; draft/07-drawings.md (FIG. 6 and FIG. 7 entries)
findings.detail: FIG. 6 is an elevation seen looking horizontally at the outer surface of a side wall. FIG-6.md places the cutting-plane line for FIG. 7 as "A horizontal broken line [that] crosses the fragment at the level of the smaller outline", with both end arrows "pointing toward the bottom of the drawing area". In an elevation, a horizontal cutting-plane line with arrows pointing down defines a horizontal cutting plane viewed from above, so FIG. 7 would have to be a plan section. FIG-7.md instead specifies a vertical elevation-section: the shell wall appears as an "upright wall body" with "its outer surface facing left and its inner surface facing right", and the latch is "A small block [that] sits above the shaft" — an above/below relationship that exists only in a vertical section. For FIG. 7 as specified, the cutting plane must be a vertical plane containing the stem axis, which appears in FIG. 6 as a vertical line, with the arrows pointing horizontally in the direction FIG. 7 is viewed. The two briefs are therefore mutually inconsistent about the same named section line. The designation itself is consistent ("7" at each end, read as line 7-7, matching "taken on line 7-7 of FIG. 6" in both FIG-7.md and draft/07-drawings.md); only the line geometry and arrow direction are wrong.
findings.evidence: figures/FIG-6.md: "A horizontal broken line crosses the fragment at the level of the smaller outline and passes across it ... Its left end carries a short arrow pointing toward the bottom of the drawing area and, beside that arrow, the section designation 7. Its right end carries a second short arrow, also pointing toward the bottom of the drawing area". figures/FIG-7.md: "A thick hatched upright wall body stands across the middle of the drawing area, its outer surface facing left and its inner surface facing right." and "A small block sits above the shaft within the outline, to the right of the coil spring".
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-6.md, replace the cutting-plane paragraph with: "A vertical broken line crosses the fragment through the smaller outline and the small square, beginning a short distance above the upper break line of the fragment and ending a short distance below its lower break line, both ends remaining well inside the drawing area. This broken line is the cutting-plane line for the sectional view FIG. 7. Its upper end carries a short arrow pointing toward the right-hand side of the drawing area and, beside that arrow, the section designation 7. Its lower end carries a second short arrow, also pointing toward the right-hand side of the drawing area, and beside that arrow the section designation 7 is repeated. Both arrows therefore point in the same direction, which is the direction in which FIG. 7 is seen, and the repeated section designation 7 at the two ends makes the cutting-plane line read line 7-7." In the same file, replace the "View designations" bullet with: "- Section designation 7: beside the arrow at the upper end of the vertical broken line, and repeated beside the arrow at the lower end, giving line 7-7 for FIG. 7." In the numerals list of figures/FIG-6.md, change the numeral 14 placement to "well inside the rectangle, clear of the smaller outline and of the vertical broken line." No change is needed to figures/FIG-7.md or draft/07-drawings.md.

findings.title: FIG. 7 shows the indicator stem projecting into the carrier interior, which is unsupported and conflicts with the no-airflow-control statement
findings.where: figures/FIG-7.md, paragraphs describing the indicator body and the shaft
findings.detail: FIG-7.md specifies that the indicator body outline extends "through the thickness of the wall body from its outer surface to its inner surface", is "open at both of its ends", and that the shaft "extends beyond both of its ends: to the left the shaft projects past the outer surface of the wall body, and to the right its inner end projects past the inner surface of the wall body." The disclosure supports only that the indicator is "visible from outside" and that the stem is "thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette"; it never states that any part of the stem enters the interior of the shell, and no such structure appears anywhere in draft/08-detailed-description.md, which says only that in the exposed position "the indicator stem 82 is visible from outside the outer shell 10". This is a relative location conveying technical substance (a member protruding into the interior space through which the side supply passages run), not a mere outline convention, and it sits in direct tension with the application's own statement that the indicator does not obstruct those passages.

An indicator stem is thermally coupled to one phase-change cassette and retained by a temperature-responsive latch."
